column5: The course names Dhar Tichitt millet from about 1500 BCE as the clear Saharan farming case. MacDonald, Champion and Manning report the earliest morphologically domestic pearl millet from the Lower Tilemsi Valley, Mali, at 2500 to 2000 BCE (from Manning and colleagues, 2011), and say these are the earliest known from Africa; Dhar Nema millet is dated 1750 to 1500 BCE and Dhars Tichitt and Oualata 1900 to 1500 BCE.

Windé Koroji Ouest: hearth charcoal 3635 plus or minus 90 bp, calibrated 2136 to 1893 BCE (one sigma); midden charcoal 3115 plus or minus 195 bp, calibrated 1612 to 1123 BCE. The midden fills the house with no change in pottery, so the authors doubt a thousand-year occupation and suggest a limited extension, perhaps to 1400 BCE. A worked example of reading dates.

Method: 26 litres of soil in ten samples, bucket flotation on a 0.25 mm mesh, 197 grains and fruit remains identified. Direct AMS dating of two millet grains in 1994 failed for too little carbon, so the early millet date rests on 17 pearl-millet seeds found in all three phases including the early hearth, not on a date of the grains.

Livestock: domestic sheep in the earliest phase (3 per cent of mammal remains, 6 per cent with sheep-or-goat); cattle from about 1600 BCE (23 per cent, over 40 per cent with Bovinae); warthog over 75 per cent of mammals in the earliest phase. Cattle were questioned as possibly African buffalo and the authors separated them by bone shape (Bos versus Syncerus).

Around 2000 BCE groups at Windé Koroji and in the Lower Tilemsi had a flexible economy of hunting, fishing, millet and gathered fruit, with herd mixes that varied, unlike Inland Niger Delta specialists who traded with each other.
Current climate conditions began not long after about 2000 BCE; at the site the setting was more humid, a gallery forest, which fits the course's drying Sahara.

Foreword by Y. A. Usman (National Commission for Museums and Monuments, Abuja): Nok Culture 1500 to 0 BCE, about 350 sites documented and about 80 excavated, project begun 2005; the first hypothesis that Nok art and early iron came from a complex society changed with the results; the Dufuna canoe, found in the Lake Chad work, is the oldest boat from Africa. The course dates Nok mainly to the first millennium BCE and the early centuries CE.

The contents list a chapter by Franke and Beck, 'Early Nok or Not?', on linking second-millennium BCE sites in central Nigeria to Nok. Only the title is in the ingested pages, so the 1500 BCE start is a debated claim here.
